title: UN Endorses Map Showing Africa's True Size
paragraphs: The United Nations General Assembly has formally endorsed the use of a world map that more accurately reflects the true size of Africa, a decision that supporters have described as a historic step toward correcting centuries of distortion.

On September 4, 2026, the General Assembly adopted a resolution known as "Correct the Map" by 164 votes to one, with six abstentions. The resolution was introduced by Togo on behalf of the African Group, which represents the 54 African member states at the UN, and it was supported by the African Union. The United States cast the only vote against it.

At the center of the debate is the Mercator projection, which was created by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569. Designed primarily for navigation, the Mercator map preserves the shapes of landmasses but significantly distorts their sizes, making regions close to the poles appear far larger than they really are. As a result, Greenland and Africa look roughly the same size on a Mercator map, even though Africa is about 14 times larger.

The resolution encourages the wider use of equal-area projections, such as the Equal Earth map, which was developed in 2018 by Tom Patterson, Bernhard Jenny and Bojan Šavrič. This projection shows the relative sizes of countries and continents more accurately, although it slightly distorts their shapes.

Importantly, the resolution is not legally binding. It does not ban the Mercator projection or require anyone to abandon it. Instead, the African Union said the resolution promotes equal-area maps in classrooms, the media and international institutions.

Togo's Foreign Minister, Robert Dussey, argued that maps shape the way people understand the world. Carlos Lopes, a professor at the University of Cape Town who supported the campaign, called it an emotional day.
However, not everyone welcomed the decision. A US representative, Yaryna Ferencevych, criticized the resolution as ideological.
